title: What did reading ever do for us?
gist: Alastair Benn accepts James Marriott's alarm in 'The New Dark Ages' about a post-literate society but attacks its core accounting: the Terror, the Vendee, Fascism and Communism were products of the literate mentality too, so mass literacy cannot be scored as net-positive by omitting its costs. He also supplies the practical rebuttal Marriott lacks - dumbed-down phones and timed lock boxes work, and demand for them is growing, with the UK accounting for half of one Spanish maker's sales.

insights.claim: James Marriott dates the high tide of literacy from the 18th century to roughly the mid-20th century before television, arguing it produced genuine mass democracy ruled by elites capable of making it work and of correcting their own mistakes.
insights.speaker: Alastair Benn
insights.so_what: Establishes the benchmark period against which declinist arguments about attention and governance are being measured.
insights.quote: It was an era of genuine mass democracy ruled by elites capable of making it work.
insights.locator: That historical moment – running roughly to the middle of the 20th century

insights.claim: Marriott's mechanism is that only reading - not moving image or sound - amplifies pattern-spotting and expands cognitive flexibility, because the book introduced a model of behaviour that was concentrated, immersive and personal.
insights.speaker: Alastair Benn
insights.so_what: The medium-specificity claim is the load-bearing element; if it fails, the whole decline argument becomes a claim about time allocation rather than cognition.
insights.quote: Neither the moving image nor sound achieves these effects.

insights.claim: Marriott marshals a convincing range of international measures showing the smartphone generation struggles with IQ, practical intelligence and pattern-spotting tests - precisely the qualities cultivated by reading.
insights.speaker: Alastair Benn
insights.so_what: A reviewer hostile to the book's framing still concedes the measurement evidence, which strengthens the case that measured cognitive decline is real.
insights.quote: He marshals a convincing range of international measures that show that the smartphone generation struggles with cognitive tests – IQ, practical intelligence, pattern-spotting
insights.locator: But Marriott certainly captures something alarming

insights.claim: Nicholas Carr's 2010 worry in The Shallows about hyperlink-following now seems quaint, because the surfing and blogging era was superseded within a decade by an audiovisual carnival of swiping and short video.
insights.speaker: Alastair Benn
insights.so_what: Attention-economy critiques age fast; assume today's concerns will be superseded by a further step-change in format within a similar timeframe.
insights.quote: That now seems quaint – minor stuff, and the substance of a million water cooler conversations
insights.locator: These arguments will be familiar to readers of Nicholas Carr

insights.claim: The Terror's architects - Saint-Just and Robespierre - carried the mark of highly literate minds, and have as good a claim to represent the Enlightenment as the more palatable Voltaire, which makes a purely positive accounting of mass literacy untenable.
insights.speaker: Alastair Benn
insights.so_what: The central counter-thesis: any narrative that credits a technology only with its benefits is systematically mispricing it.
insights.quote: Saint-Just and Robespierre have as good and as sincere a claim to represent the Enlightenment as the, to modern eyes, more palatable Voltaire.
insights.locator: Literacy underpinned the less savoury side

insights.claim: Fascism and Communism are both incomprehensible without the literate mentality, and the will to impose ideological schemata over entire peoples 'was brought to perfection in some of the most literate societies in history'.
insights.speaker: Alastair Benn
insights.so_what: Inverts the standard techno-optimist mapping: higher information capability enabled the 20th century's most systematic atrocities, not just its progress.
insights.quote: The will to impose ideological schemata upon great swathes of space, over entire peoples, was brought to perfection in some of the most literate societies in history.
insights.locator: The cult of reason, formulated by men

insights.claim: The excesses and the achievements of the literate age cannot be separated because both were products of literacy - the European novel and the Vendee massacres issue from the same capability.
insights.speaker: Alastair Benn
insights.so_what: A general-purpose template for assessing any transformative technology: the upside and downside cases share a mechanism and cannot be separately underwritten.
insights.quote: But it is too easy to separate the excesses from the achievements. Both were products of literacy.
insights.locator: The age of literacy had its great achievements

insights.claim: Marriott's history of literacy omits both the Wars of Religion that preceded it and the Terror that followed, and his story simply does not continue beyond 1789 - a selection that produces a reassuring rather than accurate account.
insights.speaker: Alastair Benn
insights.so_what: A specific, checkable claim about where a popular declinist argument truncates its evidence - the kind of framing flaw worth looking for in any trend thesis.
insights.quote: The flaw is that the story is told partially and with two significant omissions: the Wars of Religion that lay far back in the country’s past and the Terror that was still to come.
insights.locator: In accounting for the origins of mass literacy

insights.claim: The intensely literate European bourgeoisie depicted in Proust were ill-prepared for the age that followed and their class largely did not survive it - literacy conferred no protection against the 20th century.
insights.speaker: Alastair Benn
insights.so_what: Cultural capital is not a hedge against regime change; a caution against assuming educated elites will navigate disruption successfully.
insights.quote: Intensely cultivated, intensely literate, these charming representatives of the European bourgeoisie were ill-prepared for the age that followed. Their class largely did not survive it.
insights.locator: It is a conversation that is imagined

insights.claim: Montaigne, enlisted by Marriott as an early harbinger of the literacy revolution, was in fact a practising Catholic all his life who remained silent in matters of deepest conscience - a wise course amid vicious accusations of heresy.
insights.speaker: Alastair Benn
insights.so_what: Warns against retroactively recruiting historical figures into present-day intellectual lineages - a common error in trend narratives.
insights.quote: In matters of deepest conscience, Montaigne remained silent. Amid vicious accusations of heresy and counter-heresy, it was a wise course of action.

insights.claim: Even the most literate man of his day accepted that knowledge was only useful if used well or deliberately circumscribed - a constraint the author says is worth keeping in mind through every later stage of the literacy story.
insights.speaker: Alastair Benn
insights.so_what: Reusable principle for information-abundance debates: the value of knowledge depends on deliberate limitation, not maximal access.
insights.quote: Even the most literate man of his day accepted that knowledge was only useful if it was used well, or deliberately circumscribed.
insights.locator: Even the most literate man of his day

themes.theme: Attention technology has a supply side

insights.claim: Marriott is wrong that smartphone users can do nothing, because practical solutions have emerged since he wrote - the author uses a Balance Phone, made by a Spanish company that reverse-engineers Android to make it impossible to download entertainment apps like YouTube, Instagram and Twitter while keeping WhatsApp, email and news.
insights.speaker: Alastair Benn
insights.so_what: A live consumer category is forming in response to attention capture - hardware and software that deliberately subtracts function is becoming a product niche.
insights.quote: My smartphone is a Balance Phone, produced by a Spanish company which reverse-engineers Android systems to make it impossible to download ‘entertaining’ apps such as YouTube, Instagram and Twitter.
insights.locator: But he is wrong to argue that there is nothing

insights.claim: Demand for deliberately restricted phones is growing, the product now sells worldwide, and 50 per cent of its sales are accounted for by the UK market.
insights.speaker: Alastair Benn
insights.so_what: A concrete demand signal and an unusually concentrated geography - the UK is the lead market for anti-attention hardware.
insights.quote: Demand is growing. The product now sells worldwide – and 50 per cent of its sales are accounted for by the UK market.

insights.claim: Well-paid Silicon Valley engineers have designed smartphones to win an ever-increasing portion of attention and are very good at their jobs - which Marriott takes as proof of irresistibility but which the author treats as a design problem with counter-designs available.
insights.speaker: Alastair Benn
insights.so_what: Framing attention capture as engineered rather than inevitable is what opens the market for counter-products and, eventually, regulation.
insights.quote: well-paid Silicon Valley engineers have designed smartphones to win an ever-increasing portion of our attention; and they are very good at their jobs
insights.locator: As he points out, well-paid Silicon Valley engineers

insights.claim: The smartphone revolution is global and its effects outside the developed West are entirely different - the journeys of migrants who walk across deserts and sail to Europe are inconceivable without the smartphone, a dimension the book ignores.
insights.speaker: Alastair Benn
insights.so_what: Attention-decline arguments are a rich-world framing; the same technology functions as critical infrastructure elsewhere, including for migration flows into Europe.
insights.quote: The journeys of the men and women who walk across deserts and sail the high seas to arrive on the shores of Europe are inconceivable without the smartphone.
insights.locator: The effects of the smartphone might be experienced here

insights.claim: Marriott's claim that cinema is an art form 'hopelessly trapped in the exterior world of surfaces' erects a general standard on a foundation of personal taste, which the author rejects by citing lasting insights from Tarkovsky, Rohmer and Powell and Pressburger.
insights.speaker: Alastair Benn
insights.so_what: Ranking media by depth is unfalsifiable preference dressed as analysis - a caution when declinist arguments depend on medium hierarchies.
insights.quote: Provocation can be part of the work of criticism, but erecting a general standard on a foundation of personal taste is risky.
insights.locator: Marriott concludes by raising the stakes

insights.claim: The open question the book leaves unanswered is whether any society has ever found a happy medium between what it reads and how it lives - framing the attention problem as permanent rather than newly created by the smartphone.
insights.speaker: Alastair Benn
insights.so_what: If the imbalance between consumption and living is perennial, current alarm is a recurring cycle rather than a unique inflection - a discount to apply to decline narratives.
insights.quote: have we ever found a happy medium between what we read and how we live?
insights.locator: The other half of the conundrum is left unanswered
